canonicalName: Complex numbers as points of the plane and as two-dimensional real algebra

milestones.label: Wallis anticipates a plane picture
milestones.work: John Wallis, A Treatise of Algebra, 1685
milestones.description: Wallis's algebra treatise is said to have foreshadowed the idea of a complex number as a point in a plane, though not developed.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia notes the plane idea was anticipated in Wallis's 1685 algebra treatise and that Wessel first described it in 1799.

milestones.note: Wikipedia statement only; Wallis text not checked.

milestones.label: Wessel's memoir on the analytic representation of direction
milestones.work: Caspar Wessel, Om directionens analytiske betegning, Nye Samling af det Kongelige Danske Videnskabernes Selskabs Skrifter 5, 1799
milestones.description: A Norwegian surveyor published a geometric way to add and multiply directed line segments, equivalent to the complex plane, which went unnoticed for about a century.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says the geometric interpretation was first published by Wessel: paper submitted to the Danish Academy 10 March 1797, printed 1799, rediscovered 1895.
Wikipedia gives Wessel 1799 for the first description of a complex number as a plane point.
Wessel biography confirms he invented the geometric representation before Argand.

milestones.note: No Crossref/archive.org record located for the 1799 volume; year rests on three history pages that agree. Memoir read 1797, printed 1799; publication year used.

milestones.label: Argand's Essai on imaginary quantities in geometric constructions
milestones.work: Jean-Robert Argand, Essai sur une manière de représenter les quantités imaginaires dans les constructions géométriques, Paris, 1806 (small private printing; 2nd ed. Hoüel 1874)
milestones.description: Argand independently gave the rotation-by-90-degrees reading of i and the modulus, and his name became attached to the diagram.

evidence.claim: Argand produced the geometric interpretation in a memoir of 1806, possibly privately printed; copies circulated 1806-1813.
A 1874 edition of the Essai exists, evidence for the work and title but not for the 1806 date.

milestones.note: Whether the 1806 memoir was properly published is uncertain per MacTutor; also the standard biography of Argand is doubted.

milestones.label: Gauss publishes his theory of complex numbers as plane points
milestones.work: Carl Friedrich Gauss, Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, commentatio secunda, Gottingische gelehrte Anzeigen 1831
milestones.description: Gauss overcame earlier doubts, presented complex numbers as points of the plane and fixed much of the modern notation and vocabulary.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia says Gauss published his treatment of complex numbers as plane points in 1831, largely fixing modern notation and terminology.

milestones.note: Work citation from memory; year 1831 is from Wikipedia. No bibliographic record checked.

milestones.label: Hamilton presents complex numbers as ordered pairs
milestones.work: W. R. Hamilton, paper read to the Royal Irish Academy, 4 Nov 1833
milestones.description: Hamilton read a paper treating complex numbers as couples of real numbers with algebraic rules, later printed.

evidence.claim: MacTutor reports the 4 November 1833 reading expressing complex numbers as algebraic couples, and the 1835 BAAS paper on algebra as the science of pure time.

milestones.note: A reading, not a printing; the printed version is the 1837 milestone.

milestones.label: Hamilton's Theory of Conjugate Functions, or Algebraic Couples
milestones.work: W. R. Hamilton, Theory of Conjugate Functions, or Algebraic Couples; with a Preliminary and Elementary Essay on Algebra as the Science of Pure Time, Trans. Royal Irish Academy 17, 1837
milestones.description: The printed memoir defined complex numbers as ordered pairs of reals with sum and product rules, giving a purely algebraic foundation.

evidence.claim: The article is in Transactions of the Royal Irish Academy volume 17, whose volume record is dated 1837.
evidence.source: Internet Archive items (volume and JSTOR article records)

evidence.claim: The JSTOR article record carries the full title and volume 17.

milestones.note: The archive.org JSTOR item shows a placeholder date 1831-01-01; volume 17 is 1837 per the volume record. Crossref has no record.

works.whyItMatters: First publication of the geometric representation.

canonicalName: Impossibility of solving the general quintic by radicals

milestones.label: Lagrange's analysis of methods for solving equations
milestones.work: J.-L. Lagrange, Reflexions sur la resolution algebrique des equations, Nouv. Mem. Acad. Berlin, c. 1770-71
milestones.description: Lagrange unified known solution methods through resolvents and permutations of roots, hinting that degree five might be out of reach.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia dates Lagrange's groundwork to around 1770 and calls it a precursor of Galois theory without a proof of impossibility.
MacTutor stresses Lagrange still hoped to solve the quintic and that Ruffini built on his reflections.

milestones.note: Wikipedia says 'around 1770'; imprint year of the memoir not checked.

milestones.label: Ruffini's Teoria generale delle equazioni
milestones.work: Paolo Ruffini, Teoria generale delle equazioni, in cui si dimostra impossibile la soluzione algebraica delle equazioni generali di grado superiore al quarto, Bologna, 1799
milestones.description: Ruffini published the first claimed proof that the general equation of degree above four has no solution by radicals; the proof had a gap.

evidence.claim: Library record for the book, Bologna 1799.
MacTutor: Ruffini's 1799 book claimed unsolvability of the quintic by radicals; one gap remains.
Wikipedia: first nearly proved by Ruffini in 1799.

milestones.label: Permutation-group reasoning applied to the quintic
milestones.work: Paolo Ruffini, Teoria generale delle equazioni, 1799
milestones.description: The same book first used order, cycle structure, conjugacy and primitivity of permutation groups to attack an equation-solving question.

evidence.claim: MacTutor states Ruffini used group theory, having to invent it, and lists the notions he introduced.

milestones.note: Same book as the first_statement: it truly plays both roles (statement of impossibility; first use of the permutation technique).

milestones.label: Ruffini's later proofs and Cauchy's permutation work
milestones.work: P. Ruffini, further proofs 1808 and 1813; A.-L. Cauchy, memoirs on permutations c. 1813-1815
milestones.description: Ruffini refined the argument and Cauchy, influenced by him, developed permutation groups and endorsed the result.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: further proofs in 1808 and 1813; the 1813 one resembles what later was called Wantzel's modification; Cauchy wrote on permutation groups 1813-1815 and called the proof complete.

milestones.label: Abel's privately printed proof
milestones.work: N. H. Abel, Memoire sur les equations algebriques ou l'on demontre l'impossibilite de la resolution de l'equation generale du cinquieme degre, Christiania, 1824
milestones.description: Abel proved the impossibility for the general fifth-degree equation in a short pamphlet printed at his own expense.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: in 1824 he proved the impossibility, publishing in French at his own expense.
Wikipedia gives Abel a proof in 1824.
A German translation of this title appears in an 1889 collection (confirms the title, not the 1824 date).

milestones.label: Abel's proof in Crelle's Journal
milestones.work: N. H. Abel, Beweis der Unmoglichkeit, algebraische Gleichungen von hoheren Graden als dem vierten allgemein aufzulosen, J. reine angew. Math. 1 (1826) 65-84
milestones.description: A clearer version of the proof appeared in the first volume of Crelle's new journal, making it widely accessible.

evidence.claim: Crossref record: Journal fur die reine und angewandte Mathematik, 1826, pages 65-84.
MacTutor: Crelle encouraged a clearer version, which appeared in his journal.

milestones.label: Wantzel's simplified proof
milestones.work: P. L. Wantzel, new proof of the impossibility of solving all algebraic equations by radicals, 1845
milestones.description: Wantzel gave a tighter version of Abel's argument, citing both Abel and Ruffini.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: in 1845 Wantzel gave a new proof, remarking that Abel's was correct but too complicated and Ruffini's insufficient.
MacTutor Ruffini page says the 1813 Ruffini proof is essentially Wantzel's modification published in 1845.

milestones.note: Venue of the Wantzel paper not verified; year from MacTutor.

milestones.label: Jordan publishes a systematic treatise on substitutions and algebraic equations
milestones.work: Jordan, C., Traite des substitutions et des equations algebriques, 1870
milestones.description: Monograph that develops group-theoretic methods for algebraic equations, including the unsolvability of the general quintic.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists the treatise with first publication year 1870

milestones.note: Year from catalogue; the claim that it is the first systematic treatment of this result was not checked against a survey.

works.citation: Teoria generale delle equazioni
works.whyItMatters: First attempted proof of unsolvability of the quintic, with permutation-group ideas.

works.citation: Beweis der Unmoglichkeit... (J. reine angew. Math. 1)
Reflexions sur la resolution algebrique des equations
works.whyItMatters: Resolvent and permutation analysis behind Ruffini and Abel.

works.citation: Memoirs on permutations
works.whyItMatters: Developed permutation groups and endorsed Ruffini.

works.citation: New proof of impossibility by radicals

notes: Ruffini's 1799 book carries both the first statement and the first permutation-group application, which is one work in two roles. Main gaps: the Lagrange 1770 imprint is unchecked and the Wantzel 1845 venue is not verified.

canonicalName: Fourier series: from heat flow to analysis

milestones.label: Fourier's memoir on heat propagation in solid bodies
milestones.work: J. Fourier, memoire sur la propagation de la chaleur dans les corps solides, read to the Paris Institute 21 December 1807
milestones.description: Fourier used sums of sines and cosines to solve the heat equation for a solid, the purpose that created the theory.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: work began around 1804; the 1807 memoir was read on 21 December 1807, with Lagrange and Laplace objecting to its generality and rigour.
Wikipedia says the memoir introduced Fourier series for the heat equation.

milestones.note: Memoir was read, not printed at the time; full printing came much later (not checked), so it is not used as first_statement. Reclassified from first_application to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1822) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Paris Institute prize for the theory of heat
milestones.work: Fourier's prize essay, 1811
milestones.description: The Institute's prize on heat propagation was awarded to Fourier, though the report criticised rigour.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: the 1811 prize subject was heat propagation in solids and Fourier's essay won, with reservations.

milestones.note: Reclassified from recognition to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1822) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Theorie analytique de la chaleur
milestones.work: Joseph Fourier, Theorie analytique de la chaleur, Paris, 1822
milestones.description: The book printed Fourier's method: arbitrary functions represented by trigonometric series, with the heat equation as the motivating problem; it is also his systematic treatment.

evidence.claim: Library record, Paris 1822.
MacTutor: the Academy published his prize essay as the Analytical Theory of Heat in 1822.
Wikipedia dates the treatise to 1822.

milestones.note: Plays both first printed statement and first systematic treatment; consolidation not listed separately. Bessel used Fourier series for Kepler's equation in work published 1819 (Wikipedia), independent and earlier in print but not about heat; left as a note, not a milestone.

milestones.label: Dirichlet's convergence theorem
milestones.work: P. G. L. Dirichlet, Sur la convergence des series trigonometriques qui servent a representer une fonction arbitraire entre des limites donnees, J. reine angew. Math. 4 (1829) 157-169
milestones.description: Dirichlet gave the first rigorous sufficient conditions for a Fourier series to converge to its function.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, Crelle's Journal 1829, pages 157-169.
Wikipedia notes Dirichlet and Riemann later put Fourier's results on precise footing.

milestones.note: Characterisation of the theorem content is from memory of the title and Wikipedia's remark.

milestones.label: Riemann's habilitation on trigonometric series
milestones.work: B. Riemann, Habilitation dissertation on representability of functions by trigonometric series, completed 1854 (printed 1867)
milestones.description: Riemann studied which functions are integrable and the converse question of what a trigonometric series says about its function.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: after thirty months of work the dissertation defined integrability (Riemann integral) and asked the reverse question for trigonometric series.
Volume 13 of the Gottingen Abhandlungen (1866-67) record exists; the paper's inclusion there is from memory.

milestones.note: Year is the completion year, not the 1867 print year; print venue not verified.

milestones.label: Trigonometric series in the vibrating-string problem
milestones.work: Euler, d'Alembert, D. Bernoulli, mid-18th century
milestones.description: Earlier work on wave motion used trigonometric sums, providing the toolkit Fourier generalised.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia names Euler, d'Alembert and Daniel Bernoulli as having done preliminary investigations before Fourier.

milestones.note: Exact dates not established here; unknown year allowed for a precursor.

Habilitation on trigonometric series

milestones.work: A.-L. Cauchy, memoir on definite integrals presented 1814

evidence.claim: MacTutor: he began a study of the calculus of residues in 1826 in this work.

milestones.label: Complex function of a complex variable defined
milestones.work: A.-L. Cauchy, Lecons sur le calcul differentiel, 1829
milestones.description: Cauchy gave, for the first time per MacTutor, a definition of a complex function of a complex variable.

evidence.claim: MacTutor attributes the first definition of a complex function of a complex variable to the 1829 lectures.

milestones.label: Cauchy's Lecons sur le calcul differentiel
milestones.work: A.-L. Cauchy, Lecons sur le calcul differentiel, Paris, 1829
milestones.description: Textbook in which Cauchy defines a complex function of a complex variable, so it also consolidates the subject.

evidence.claim: Open Library record of the 1829 Lecons sur le calcul differentiel.
Cauchy defined a complex function of a complex variable for the first time in a textbook in 1829.

milestones.note: Same book as the existing 1829 key_development; the consolidation role is added because it is the textbook treatment. Drop one role if the duplicate is unwanted.

milestones.description: Goursat proved the integral theorem assuming only that the complex derivative exists.

Wikipedia: Goursat showed the theorem holds with only a derivative existing.

milestones.label: Gauss's general investigations of curved surfaces
milestones.work: C. F. Gauss, Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas, 1828
milestones.description: Gauss developed intrinsic curvature of surfaces, the starting point for Riemann's generalisation.

evidence.claim: Contemporary 1828 account of the Gauss paper with this title.
Wikipedia calls Riemannian geometry a broad generalisation of the differential geometry of surfaces in R^3.

milestones.note: The Crossref item is a review of Gauss's paper, which dates the work to 1828.

milestones.label: Riemann's habilitation lecture
milestones.work: B. Riemann, Ueber die Hypothesen, welche der Geometrie zu Grunde liegen, lecture of 10 June 1854
milestones.description: Riemann introduced n-dimensional manifolds with a metric from a quadratic form in an oral lecture chosen by Gauss.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: delivered 10 June 1854 after Gauss chose it among three lectures.
Wikipedia says Riemannian manifolds were first conceptualised by Riemann in 1854.

milestones.note: Oral and unpublished until after his death; the printed paper is the first_statement.

milestones.label: Riemann's lecture is printed
milestones.work: B. Riemann, Ueber die Hypothesen, welche der Geometrie zu Grunde liegen, Abhandlungen der Koniglichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Gottingen 13, printed 1868
milestones.description: The lecture, written in 1854, reached print only in 1868, two years after Riemann's death.

evidence.claim: MacTutor image caption: written in 1854 but not published until 1868.
Gottingen Abhandlungen volume 13 record (dated 1866-67 by the library item).

milestones.note: The archive item calls the volume 1866; the printing is generally dated 1868 (MacTutor). Inclusion of the lecture in that volume is from memory.

milestones.label: Christoffel's transformation of quadratic differential forms
milestones.work: E. B. Christoffel, Ueber die Transformation der homogenen Differentialausdruecke zweiten Grades, J. reine angew. Math. 70 (1869) 46-70
milestones.description: Christoffel supplied the invariant machinery for quadratic differential expressions that underlies covariant differentiation.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, Crelle's Journal 1869, pages 46-70.

milestones.note: Importance (Christoffel symbols) is from memory; the title matches the topic.

milestones.label: Ricci and Levi-Civita's absolute differential calculus
milestones.work: G. Ricci and T. Levi-Civita, Methodes de calcul differentiel absolu et leurs applications, Math. Ann. 54 (1900) 125-201
milestones.description: The paper organised tensor calculus on Riemannian spaces into a systematic tool.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, Mathematische Annalen 54, 1900, pages 125-201.

milestones.note: Treated as consolidation of the calculus, not of Riemann's original ideas.

milestones.label: General relativity formulated in Riemannian terms
milestones.work: A. Einstein, Die Grundlage der allgemeinen Relativitaetstheorie, Ann. Phys. 354 (1916) 769-822
milestones.description: Einstein used the geometry of a four-dimensional metric manifold to formulate gravity.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, Annalen der Physik 354, 1916, pages 769-822.
Wikipedia: Riemannian geometry enabled the formulation of Einstein's general relativity.

milestones.note: Earlier Einstein-Grossmann work (1913) not checked and so not listed.

works.citation: Ueber die Hypothesen, welche der Geometrie zu Grunde liegen
Disquisitiones generales circa superficies curvas
Ueber die Transformation der homogenen Differentialausdruecke zweiten Grades
Methodes de calcul differentiel absolu et leurs applications (with Ricci)

notes: Riemann's 1854 lecture is a precursor, and under the schema rule the 1868 printing is the first statement. Main uncertainty: the print volume is dated 1866 by the archive record and 1868 by MacTutor, and the Christoffel and Einstein-Grossmann links are from memory.
searchedSources: Wikipedia saved lead and raw: Riemannian manifold, Riemannian geometry

canonicalName: Abel: elliptic functions as inverses of elliptic integrals

milestones.label: Legendre's work on elliptic integrals
milestones.work: A.-M. Legendre, Exercices de calcul integral, volumes 1811, 1817, 1819
milestones.description: Legendre set out the theory of elliptic integrals that Abel and Jacobi then inverted.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Legendre's main work on elliptic functions is in the three volumes of the Exercices of 1811, 1817 and 1819.
MacTutor topic page: elliptic integrals studied since Wallis (1655); terminology changed over time.

milestones.label: Abel's Recherches sur les fonctions elliptiques, part one
milestones.work: N. H. Abel, Recherches sur les fonctions elliptiques, J. reine angew. Math. 2 (1827) 101-181
milestones.description: Abel inverted elliptic integrals to obtain doubly periodic elliptic functions.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, Crelle's Journal 1827, pages 101-181.
MacTutor: Abel turned the theory of elliptic integrals into that of elliptic functions by using inverse functions.
Wikipedia: Abel discovered elliptic functions by taking the inverse of the elliptic integral.

milestones.label: Recherches, continuation
milestones.work: N. H. Abel, Recherches sur les fonctions elliptiques (suite), J. reine angew. Math. 3 (1828) 160-190
milestones.description: The second part of the memoir carried the theory further.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, Crelle's Journal 1828, pages 160-190, marked as the continuation.

milestones.label: Legendre's praise of Abel and Jacobi
milestones.work: letter of A.-M. Legendre to Jacobi, 9 February 1828
milestones.description: Legendre saluted two young mathematicians who were advancing the branch of analysis he had long studied.

evidence.claim: MacTutor quotes the 9 February 1828 letter placing both young men among the best analysts of the era.

milestones.label: Abel's Precis d'une theorie des fonctions elliptiques
milestones.work: N. H. Abel, Precis d'une theorie des fonctions elliptiques, J. reine angew. Math. 4 (1829) 236-277 and 309-348
milestones.description: A fuller presentation of the theory appeared in two parts in the following year.

evidence.claim: Crossref records for both parts, Crelle's Journal 1829.

milestones.label: Jacobi proposes the name elliptic functions
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum, 1829
milestones.description: Jacobi's 1829 suggestion that the inverse functions of elliptic integrals be called elliptic functions, the name still in use.

evidence.claim: Following a suggestion of Jacobi in 1829, the inverse functions are now called elliptic functions.
Open Library record of the 1829 Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum.

milestones.note: Naming year is the 1829 suggestion; the wording of the suggestion itself was not read in the 1829 text.

works.citation: Recherches sur les fonctions elliptiques
Precis d'une theorie des fonctions elliptiques
Note sur les fonctions elliptiques, Crelle 3
Exercices de calcul integral

notes: Abel's 1827 statement and the 1828 and 1829 continuations are high confidence. Abel and Jacobi worked in parallel, so priority is shared in effect, and Gauss's unpublished earlier work is not among the milestones.
searchedSources: MacTutor: Abel, Jacobi, Legendre, Elliptic functions topic

canonicalName: Jacobi: theta functions and elliptic function theory

milestones.label: Jacobi's letter to Legendre
milestones.work: letter of C. G. J. Jacobi to A.-M. Legendre, 5 August 1827
milestones.description: A private letter first told Legendre of Jacobi's new advances on elliptic functions.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: on 5 August 1827 Jacobi wrote to Legendre, who saw at once that a fundamental advance had been made.

milestones.note: Private letter, so a precursor.

milestones.label: Jacobi's first printed announcement
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Extraits de deux lettres de Mr. Jacobi a l'editeur, Astronomische Nachrichten 6, pp. 33-37
milestones.description: Extracts of two letters printed in Schumacher's journal announced Jacobi's results on elliptic functions.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, Astronomische Nachrichten volume 6, pages 33-37 (record date January 1828).

milestones.note: Crossref dates the item January 1828, the volume began in 1827; the exact issue date is unresolved. Content of the extracts (theta not necessarily included) was not read. Reclassified from key_development to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1829) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Note sur les fonctions elliptiques
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Note sur les fonctions elliptiques, J. reine angew. Math. 3 (1828) 192-195
milestones.description: A short note in Crelle's Journal continued the announcement of the new theory.

evidence.claim: Crossref record, Crelle's Journal 1828, pages 192-195.

milestones.note: Reclassified from key_development to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1829) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum, Regiomonti, 1829
milestones.description: Jacobi's treatise built elliptic function theory on four theta functions.

evidence.claim: Library records for the 1829 book.
MacTutor: the theory was based on four theta functions in this paper of 1829.
Wikipedia attaches the name Jacobi to the theta function.

milestones.label: Fundamenta nova as the systematic treatise
milestones.work: C. G. J. Jacobi, Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum, 1829
milestones.description: The same book is the first systematic account of the theory.

evidence.claim: MacTutor describes the work and its later supplements as fundamental contributions to elliptic function theory.

milestones.note: Same book as the first_statement; it plays both roles.

works.citation: Fundamenta nova theoriae functionum ellipticarum
Note sur les fonctions elliptiques
Exercices de calcul integral
Recherches sur les fonctions elliptiques

notes: Jacobi's 1829 Fundamenta nova is both the first statement and the systematic treatise. Main gaps: the issue date of the 1827 announcement is unresolved, and the number-theory use of theta series is unverified, so it is not a milestone.
searchedSources: Wikipedia raw: Theta function, Jacobi elliptic functions
